game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
If there were a "maybe" option for recommending this game I would have given it that, but with only a "yes" or "no" choice unfortunately I have to just come down on the side of the latter.

This game is essentially a "choose your own adventure" detective novel wherein your decisions are all made by choosing which information to share with - or conceal from - the authorities. The concept is an interesting one and the game does throw up some nice surprises in both the gameplay and the plot, and there are occasional moments of humour.

However, the limitations in using conflicting information are rather annoying. For example sometimes the game will let you choose only one of two (or more) different pieces of information even when both are true and could be vital to successfully completing your objectives. (I get that this is a key game mechanic, but I think it could be explained or handled better to make the game feel less forced.) In particular there is one key decision which just comes down to a 50/50 guess with no supporting information to help the player make the correct choice. (I am talking about the part where the player must determine the third location - If I missed any clues as to which is the correct answer, somebody please tell me!)

Another major concern is the quality of the writing; whilst for the most part the writing is capable and there are some memorable moments, the writing is never compelling - I gave up reading about halfway through my first playthrough, instead just scanning text for the (conveniently highlighted) choices. Whilst I can forgive bad writing in some games, for a game that is all about the writing the standard really needs to be higher. Some of the text simply drags on too long, especially any form of dialogue (phone calls, chat text, etc.) - this is doubly annoying for dialogue as there is no way to skip it. (Usually you can just let it run in the background whilst you read other in-game documents, but be careful with this as some actions are time-critical.)

Replay value may depend how willing you are to work through the text again. Whilst it is nice to see the different outcomes your actions can have, it feels like 90% or more of the game remains identical so it becomes a slog to see the few changes or pick up achievements. Some of the achievements are so ambiguously described that the only way to complete them seems to be relying on lots of replays and blind luck, or of course walkthroughs.

It is a shame to see such a nice idea and plot wasted without sufficient polish, but if the devs learn from this I do look forward to seeing what else they can produce.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A decent enough story exploration game, but not being able to fast forward through the cripplingly slow phone/chat conversations really hampers replayability - which is a large factor in this game, having many different paths and endings that depend on your choices.
It's a shame I couldn't bring myself to sit through the same old conversations over and over to explore the rest of the game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Much less a game than an interactive story. It's a slim game with few objectives and a lot of fluff around it. The game tends to cram exposition into everything, and doesn't allow you to skip or fast-forward any of it. Utimately, while the plot is about making a god of machines, it doesn't justify its deus ex machina storytelling.

[h1]Show, Don't Tell[/h1]
I do not know who's idea it was to not allow the player to fast-forward or skip dialogue, but it was a [b]terrible[/b] decision. The sheer amount of exposition and meaningless chatter in the game is astounding. And this isn't a once or twice occurance, it's a regularly reoccuring situation where key bits of info required to advance the plot sit behind a 4 or 5 minute long unskippable dialogue sequence. And that 10+ minute bit right before the end of the game, who thought that was a good idea? And does the "administrator" need to say something every time I upload a piece of relevant info? It's like having Clippy from MS Word permanently built into the game.

Furthermore, the level of hand-holding is ridiculous. First off, for a game about parsing and collecting information, there's very little you actually have to read. The game essentially takes a big neon highlighter and highlights every single thing that might be of importance. Then, they go ahead and show you exactly where you might've missed a clue or hint. Secondly, the game has these "pivotal" moments where you have to decide which one of multiple conflicting statements is true, except that the system highlights conflicts before you even discover them. It's such a self-defeating mechanism. Imagine if the Sherlock novels had Watson discover a false clue and Sherlock responding "But Watson, that can't be the real clue cause I'm going to find the real clue on page 86!"

And if the story was entralling, and the world-building was coherent, maybe those bad gameplay elements could be overlooked. But they aren't. The plot is cheesy and the writing is lazy. How many times do you plan on having a random character with no background conveniently appear to tie-up some loose ends and then disappear forever? It's honestly kind of amazing how a game where everything you do is character building manages to have some of the most one-dimensional characters I've ever seen.

[h1]Breakdown[/h1]
[b]Pros[/b]
[olist]
    [*][b]Chapter Select:[/b] Thanks for at least not making me have to replay the whole game to get an achievement.
[/olist]
[b]Cons[/b]
[olist]
    [*][b]Don't stop users from fast-forwarding text.[/b]
    [*][b]Narrative, not Narrate:[/b] I should be able to tell when I come across an important piece of dialogue. I don't need the game to highlight it a bright color, the music to change to be all dramatic, and Clippy at the top exclaiming, "Wow! That piece of dialogue sure seems important!" *wink* *wink* *nudge* *nudge*
[/olist]
[b]Score[/b]: 2/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]English:[/b]
The idea of playing an investigator using a dystopian surveillance system is genuinely intriguing, and it did pull me in at first. But in my case, a few elements caught me off guard, and I ultimately landed on the feeling of, “Damn, this could have been great.”

You're heavily railroaded. A handler constantly directs you, and you're only allowed to submit pre-highlighted data. So even if you spot something meaningful, if it hasn’t been highlighted, it’s off-limits… unless the system decides to highlight it later. In other words, it's Orwell—not your judgment—deciding what's relevant and when.
Also, can’t look into unimportant connections, people connected to the main people you’re already watching. That undermines immersion. Information and connections that should enrich the world instead feel like empty filler, like walking through a map where only the area around your destination actually exists. It undercuts the immersion hard, and it really starts to highlight how little control the player has over the investigation. The joy of organizing fragmented data and piecing together insight, the detective puzzle vibe you’d expect, is barely there.

Even the surveillance state itself feels oddly toothless. Orwell is supposedly a powerful system, yet the most basic info must be found manually. I get that the in-game incident is Orwell's first mission, but if the game is trying to sell a functioning surveillance state, it comes off half-baked.
Starting the investigation from scratch, with no basic personal data preloaded, makes the process resemble ordinary police work more than the operation of a dystopian digital panopticon.

The system’s invasive abilities (like tapping calls or accessing private devices without consent) do hint at Orwell’s dystopian cruelty. But from the player’s point of view, Orwell never allows unrestricted monitoring. Only designated “persons of interest” can be investigated, and since the events revolve around terrorism with real casualties, even the more questionable actions can be framed as emergency measures. This waters down the ethical tension; Orwell’s moral horror feels too easy to rationalize.
Even when one character challenges the legitimacy of Orwell’s power, their argument rings hollow—coming from someone involved in a bombing, it’s hard to see them as anything other than a villain delivering a monologue.

And when the second half of the game shows [spoiler]people casually messing stuff up[/spoiler], it makes you wonder: maybe the surveillance wasn’t that tight to begin with? How effective is this Orwell network if [spoiler]people willing to say "f*ck the system" and can still go full riot mode[/spoiler]? If the system’s that fragile, then what was the point of its supposed success in lowering crime in the first place?
I couldn’t quite tell whether this game was trying to criticize the dystopia built around Orwell or somehow justify it.

Also, you can’t skip or fast-forward dialogue, which I get is supposed to simulate “real-time surveillance,” but it just kills the pacing. This took me about four hours to get through the all chapters, and the lack of any way to redo choices just makes the idea of replaying for achievements or alternate paths a hard no.

[b]日本語:[/b]
ディストピアの監視システムを用いる調査官という導入は凄く面白いし実際に惹き込まれましたが、幾つかの要素が引っ掛かって最終的に「惜しいな」という感想に着地しました。

有り体に言うと意外と(?)自由度が低い。プレイヤーが進行の主導権を握っていないというのが率直な感想です。
まずアドバイザーが就くので情報の海に放り出されて手探りで進むのではなく自然と一本道になるので未知の間を自走する楽しみが希薄です。
更に、二次的な関係者(直接の監視対象ではない人々)の情報には触れられず、例えば誰かの両親や友人等が相関図に載っても飽くまで賑やかしで、RPGで言うなら「目的地周辺だけ作ってあるマップ」みたいな印象を受けるので没入感を削がれます。
そしてOrwellでは“ハイライトされている情報だけ”が利用可能なのですが、例えば関係者の画像を見付けたから登録したいと思ってもハイライトされていないなら使えない――と思いきや後になって急にハイライトされるという事も。つまりシステム(進行度等)の都合で意味の有無が一転してしまうので「役に立つか分からないが留めておきたい」みたいな遊び方は全く想定されておらず、“調査官”という言葉から連想して捜査・整理・推理というパズル的な喜びを期待すると肩透かしを食らいます。

物語や世界観についても引っ掛かります。国民の情報がOrwellに登録されておらず、住所も電話番号も全てプレイヤーが探し出す事になるのは、ゲーム内での事案がOrwellの初陣であるにせよ監視社会のディストピアを念頭に置くなら中途半端な気がしますし、基本的な個人情報から調査となると手順に警察の捜査との差異も感じられません。
Orwellを通じた通話や情報端末への無許可でのアクセスは人権や倫理への一種の加害性というディストピアがディストピアたる所以を描写してはいますが、プレイヤーの視点では上記の通り(=重要人物以外には触れられない) 犯罪や危機の捜査にしか使われておらず、しかも問題となる事件が死傷者を伴うテロなので、倫理観を脇に置くのは超法規的措置だと補完する事も出来てしまう。
その犯人がOrwellを非難したところで犠牲者を生んだテロリストの言説として空虚に響くだけでしょう。
また[spoiler]後半での展開も炎上からの破壊行動が容易く起きるのなら[/spoiler]“監視”の程度も大した事はないのでは？と感じます。監視なんぞ知るかという人が[spoiler]暴徒化したのだとしたら[/spoiler]、そもそも犯罪率の低下とは何だったんでしょうか。
正直なところ、この作品がOrwellに在る社会構造を否定的に描いているのか肯定的に描いているのか判然としませんでした。

実績や細かい分岐の確認に改めてプレイしていたら印象も変わるのかもしれませんが、ここでシステム面が障害に。というのも、だいぶのんびりしたプレイで全5章終わらせるのに約4時間掛かったのですが、Orwellには台詞送りやスキップ機能がなく、更には選択に修正が効かない仕様なのでリプレイへの精神的なハードルが高いです。
台詞送りやスキップが無いのはリアルタイムの盗聴という表現であるにしても快適性を損ないますし、こういった部分も作品の魅力を自ら削いでいる様な感じがしてなりません。

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
While the story is interesting and I can see replayability in knowing you've made the wrong move, then creating a new profile and trying to avoid that scenario... I haven't done that. I probably won't either, because I have to agree with other players: the game guides you too much.

You're basically told where to click and when, which completely defeats the point of having all of these fun tools at your disposal--they might as well have dumped all data pieces in a list and had you click on them one by one, all after the other.

The auto-highlighting spoils the point of reading anything. The game warns you that potential choices conflict instead of letting the player decide on how thoroughly they want to investigate before submitting information. Some pieces of info feel completely useless, but your supervisor somehow decides they have more value than they should and the supervisor's decision often feels like a complete whim. And vice-versa: bits of info you feel should be important are locked away or not even meant to be accessible because the game decided "Nope, I won't even let you go into that dead-end for fun".

I guess this was worth what I paid for it... $2! and no more. This had a lot of promise but it doesn't have enough depth or freedom of choice for my tastes.

Where is the gaming industry heading anyways with such tiny games? Make this thing free. If I can get bigger better games for free, why should I pay for this?

I cannot recommend this "game" until it is finished and takes as much time as it costs in dollars in hours. Right now, should be 8 hours of gameplay but it's like 30-45min of gameplay (that's what it took me to finish both chapters... very very short chapters... game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Lot of good, but outweighed by the bad.

The game was entertaining and built on a thought-provoking premise, but the game is far too short (roughly four hours in length) and the premise of the game loses its edge when the game picks a side on the question if society should sacrifice privacy for security instead of leaving that decision up to the player.

The story is well-written but offers very little in replayability. The games premise would have room for several scenarios where the player has to puzzle together what has happened or attempt to prevent crimes from happening, placing the player in situations where he has to weigh his decision how deep into someones private-life he should go to discover the truth, and even then be left with an uncertainty that forces him to make decisions based only his own interpretation of the truth. Instead, the game presents one scenario that plays out over a five-day period. The game-mechanics themselves are not complicated and the games graphics and presentation is mostly text and still-pictures, so more scenarios should not be difficult or time-consuming to add later on.

If the game had more meat on the bones I would recommend it, but for the moment this is a brief game with little replayability, but potential for a lot more.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
TL;DR: great game buggered by stupid save system. 

Orwell is a great game, no two ways about it. Easy to get into, nice story and so forth. I didn't have a problem with any of those things, however why have I then thumbed it down? 

Simple, this game, like so many others nowadays, have decided that the only save function this game needs is an autosave, meaning there is no way of backtracking, no way of re-doing things. One slip up and the game will laugh in your face and call you a tosser for the rest of the game, because that slip-up meant you didn't achieve what you wanted to do. I know some people are okay with that, they feel it's more immersive or whatever, but for me it is just a huge annoyance. "Realism" is all well and good, but they don't make the chat convos ingame take 5 minutes per post because while that'd be realistic, it's be annoying. For me it is the same thing here and it leaves me unable to really enjoy the game because it screws me over when I can't decide which of the two vague clues are the correct one. 

It is a crying shame, it's a great game but the save system isn't fun for me at all.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
More of an immersive novel than a game, Orwell begins as a smart and thoroughly engaging experience that accurately captures the dilemma of state surveillance: The violation of privacy is bad and comes with risk, but there are still real threats that motivated the imposition of surveillance in the first place. Within this context, the events of Orwell are situated within "The Nation" - a hypothetical highly developed country saddled with all of the assets and burdens of the U.S., France, the U.K. or any similar nation. Osmotic deserves praise here - they tightly and intelligently create a nuanced setting without overburdening the player.

But the success doesn't last.

As the game progresses, Orwell begins to exhibit a grasping take on modern security that feels naive. The moderated presentation that offered a balanced dialectic fades, and the political messaging of the developers becomes increasingly heavy handed and blunt. None of this occurs in a way that is surprising or unique within the context of the public surveillance debate, it is only disappointing that they couldn't have done better.

In terms of technical game mechanics, while Orwell's gameplay is a slick, engrossing and well-crafted experience - the buyer should not expect any replay value outside of a 3-5 hour playthrough.

Leaving a negative review feels somewhat harsh, although within the context of a 91% positive title, it feels appropriate for balance. It is by no means a bad game - only one that fell frustratingly short of its potential.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Okay... I don't usually write game reviews. I generally have a pretty good idea of what I'm buying beforehand on Steam, and if a game is shit it's usually because I paid for shit. But this fucking game got me.

The biggest trick is that little "Choice Matters" tag that people gave it. I love choice games. The replay value of finding every unique ending alone usually makes it worth the price. There's also something thrilling, something special to video games, when you're able to make a choice and know it matters.

Choice doesn't matter in this game.

You do ultimately get to choose what's "shown" to your supervisor, and sometimes those choices do affect the game in some way. But you're railroaded HARD through just about every major event, forced to fight for even the smallest change in dialogue from game to game. The only half-consequential "choice" you get comes at the end, and to get there you need to sit through 2+ hours of the exact same gameplay. You might as well be buying the game to play once. If you're ok with playing once and then quitting (the game does have some beautiful artwork and some really gripping moments) then by all means do so. But if you want your choices to really matter, don't buy Orwell.

- Music is OK
- The characters are relatable

- This implementation of mass surveillance is plausible

- The web is way too small, and computer hacking is way too minimalistic to be plausible.
- The enjoyment as you progress is almost a total downward slope. I think the last episode and the ending is just not ready.
- Game lasts no more than 8 hours.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Spying on citizens of a (not-so) future dystopian society in an attempt to convict them of crimes and uncover some deeper conspiracy sounds good on paper, but does not work so well in game form; at least not if it is done like Orwell does it. For 5 hours, you read through text, sort datachunks to their respective profiles, and read unskippable text / call exchanges between the subjects. That is pretty much it. The story is a bit slow and does only gain steam in the last two episodes 4 and 5, but the "gameplay" remains the same.

Perhaps even more annoying is that there is no overall lesson to be learned here; it is very much a self-containing story with no real moral aside from the obvious and ham-fisted "government can see everything you do = bad", which does not even really stick the landing as the game actually shows a few reasons for why the government may want to do such a thing, right or not.

As a game, there is not much here aside from essentially reading a more tedious novel while constantly having to switch between profiles with little choice until the end. As a story, there is some good here, but it is not engaging enough even despite the short length.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What Orwell is?

In Orwell, you are the operator of the super software that can trace every citizen digital information, and you are after  a terrorism activist group called Thought who plans to disrupt society safety through violent manifests. Then reason behind it is fear for government peeping your personal life a la NSA/Edward Snowden case. 

My thoughts

The Detective Hacking game mode made me to instant purchase Orwell game, as it combines two of my favorites genres. However it turned out to be VERY frustrating to me.

Slow pacing: I did not expect this game to be in pace with some freaky japanese action game, however what I felt is that they tried to compensate this short game with a slow pace of events combined with tons of wall texts for you to read, search, and try to link pieces with terrorisms acts. You will spend a lot of minutes reading dialogues, text messages, emails, even facebook posts lol, and others stuff, to figure out who is who, and where to go next.

Story: It has only one mainplot, no additional stages or cases, which made me judge the worthness of this purchase. The plot is short, and again, what made it last 9 hours are a bunch of useless information that visually polluted the game, and contributed barely nothing to the storyline. You spend most of your time digging useless information that sometimes take you to nowhere and suprisingly to the next part. One example, how the US gov do not even know a US citizen full name, dob, place of work? Any normal citizen could just Google them to figure out, however you find yourself stuck into finding this information no matter what! (lol) In the beginning there was some air of suspense about some terrorism acts suspects, however at the end... it was pretty lame the way it turned out. And what is even sadder is that in the end you are not in control of how the game ends, so choices don't really matter. After finishing Orwell, you can only describe this game as a Visual Novel game, and not a Detective Hacking game.

Some small rantings regarding the storyline

Spoiler 1:  [spoiler] You are the US government and you can't access a blocked article in a blog lul. [/spoiler]

Spoiler 2:  [spoiler] You are the US government and has one of super softwares but can't even trace where the suspects are [/spoiler]

Spoiler 3:  [spoiler] How the fuck some small time hacker could crack into US government super secret software so easily? Let's hope China, N. Korea, Russia, or any other terrorism groups do not hire him! [/spoiler]


Price: It expensive to pay USD 10.00 for a game with 9 hours duration, and has ZERO replayability value. Just compare it to Stardew Valley which full price is USD 15.00, now USD 10.00 in Steam Autumn Sales, which I have played over 120 hours, and has even more hundreds of gameplay and replay...

And the only thing that you expect in this kind of game, is having to work on several complex different cases, which did not happen. Also choices did not matter in the end.

If you still don't care and want to purchase Orwell, my advice would be to wait for the Christmas sale or price drop. Peace & GG.

review_text_raw:
This one's a "buy it only on sale" for me. I would pick a neutral option were it available.

It's important to understand that Orwell is not a puzzle game inasmuch as a visual novel, and from what I understand of Steam's userbase (or at least its most vocal negative reviews), this will come as a disappointment to some people. There is very little analysis involved; you are told what and whom to investigate and any conclusions about what you discover are more or less made for you. Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You also fairly short for a $10 title, with very little replayability. Halfway through the game I still thought I was in the tutorial until I glanced at the list of achievements which indicated otherwise.

In Orwell, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a recent bombing using a top secret surveillance system also called ORWELL. Specifically, you must build profiles of potential suspects based on their social media profiles, online accounts, and personal devices. This is done by selecting relevant excerpts, called datachunks, and "uploading" them to the ORWELL server. Meanwhile, your "advisor," a man called Symes, will review what you send and make important decisions based on this info. What information you choose to upload and when you upload it will affect the lives of the people you investigate and the dangerous events unfolding in "real time."

Unfortunately, your advisor is an idiot. I mean, he seems nice enough, but he's incredibly trigger-happy, and views the act of merely uploading information to compile a detailed suspect profile as an indictment in itself. "Woah, she changed her hair color? Good info, I've just sent out the warrant for her arrest."

Because of this and other aspects of gameplay where the importance of particular actions is not especially well telegraphed, most of my game-changing decisions were followed by an "oh crap, I did not just mean to do that. I hope I can fix it later!"

When control over a sandbox environment and its inhabitants is so apparently arbitrary, your first playthrough is no longer a personal journey and a reflection of your choices. Instead it is a hilarious spectacle of disastrous butterfly effects outpacing your sad and frantic attempts at damage control. This is great in a series like Hitman, though not so much in a game trying to make a point about the deadly shortsightedness of relying on a digital panopticon.

Orwell's conceit is ultimately that even a government allowed to so thoroughly investigate its private citizens may still fail to meet the outcomes that were supposed to justify the dissolution of privacy. The truth can still elude even the most advanced surveillance systems, as it does here, and so any drastic actions carried out in the name of safety may do more harm than good.

The problem is that it tries to demonstrate this through a system made deliberately inept in the service of its plot and political message. EDIT: So I'm an idiot and apparently you can arrest the true mastermind in Episode 5 provided you have enough luck and/or second playthrough foresight. However, it's not especially intuitive (the 20 datachunk limit doesn't help!), and requires some deviation from the stated goal in a game which has been so far entirely based on completing the stated goal in some form or another and which otherwise restricts your ability to freely investigate, in that:

ORWELL will only allow access to new resources once you have added a related datachunk, and even then this selection is limited by what the clumsy "AI" (read: the story) deems relevant. The AI also determines which pieces of information are selectable for use as datachunks. The result is like a crime-solving version of Chopped, wherein you must come up with your best answer given a random handful of documents. You are only able to pursue a line of thinking that the AI believes is relevant, and the AI has been written to provide the wrong answer.

You can't get much out of the stuff you're forced to work with, either, as advisors will only let you investigate people they deem worthy at the time (rest assured you will still get the blame every time something bad happens!), and with each datachunk you index in the hopes of unlocking new documents or comments, you run the risk of your advisor making an unpredictably dangerous and irreversible decision.

As a result, Orwell depicts not so much the shortcomings of overly-invasive surveillance tech as it does the flaws in this particular system which has been deliberately badly designed.

Usually writers in the "techno-voyeurism genre" can look forward to populating a lot of fake apps and web pages with filler data which serves no plot purpose except to flesh out the in-game universe and hide easter eggs. So I understand the choice for the developers to omit that open browsing capability from a practical point of view -- but it does come at a cost to Orwell's credibility.

On the positive side, Orwell has a cute low-poly aesthetic and its UI is both visually appealing and well organized, especially given what a tremendous challenge it must have been to elegantly display so much information. The soundtrack works well and effectively manages to convey dramatic tone shifts (usually from "lalala browsing someone's timeline" to "oh NO A BOMB IS ABOUT TO GO OFF IN THIRTY SECONDS!!"). I also like that there are achievements of equal calibre for most major story outcomes, "good" or otherwise.

By all means get Orwell if you enjoy techno-voyeurism (does this genre have an actual name?); you might find it to be a fun time-waster. I might pick up season 2... on sale... eventually. I just don't think it would appeal to general audiences at its current price point, or that it's particularly effective in delivering its themes.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is not a bad game, but I do think it's overrated. It falls short as a game and as a study of the surveillance state.

The gameplay mechanics are very simple -- you go to different links and and decide whether to upload them to Orwell or not. That's all there is to gameplay. Frustratingly, I ran into a few occasions where to advance the story I had to upload a link that was not obvious as to its value. Additionally, it's silly that you can't correct events later on, even before the information is acted upon -- if you send something over it's set in stone. And I'm not talking about the conflict choices -- those actually were good and created a good choice to have to make in deciding how the fate of certain people would go. 

Some of those negatives really betrayed the gamey-ness of the system. 

But worse was the whole conceit of the game really misses on being a meditation of surveillance gone awry. For one, the investigator is not a member of The Nation, which simply wouldn't happen in the real world, so it undercuts the influence of the government. The pressure that you as the investigator feels is thus negligble (unlike something like Papers, Please). The artificiality of the Orwell setup avoids the influence of government on media or bias of investigators that is very much an issue in the real world. 

Additionally, the game seems to suggest that the mere possibility of some people being investigated without having done wrong is evil. Except, that is how criminal investigations have gone since time immemorial. You start with some clues and investigate from there which will inevitably lead to some innocent people being scrutinized (even sometimes convicted). But that is the outcome of such a human operation and is not really a result of the surveillance state. And remember, we're investigating actual crimes where innocent people died. 

The game would have been much stronger if it showed intentional abuse by the system operators, influence by the government, or the ability to enact control of a population by knowing the way they think and act (think machine learning and how well it can predict certain behaviors/beliefs in people now). Or if the act in question was more dubious in nature, was maybe a false flag, or at least had some element of a frame up instead of an actual terrorist act committed by a true believer.

Another minor gripe is that you can't skip ahead on any chat or phone calls, which are interminably slow. While that might be realistic, it's also a bit boring.

The story also provides choices and branches in the same manner as a Telltale game, so if you like that facade you won't be bothered here. However, I did find it a bit unsatisfying that no matter the choices you made, the next episode would essentialy go the same way. And since everything is told in documents, calls, and chats, it's really lacking the dramatic power that a good Telltale game can have.

It wasn't a bad time but I definitely felt underwhelmed.

[h1]Overall Rating[/h1] 
[b]★★☆☆☆[/b]

[u]What I liked[/u]
[list]
  [*] The Story
  [*] The Character Building
[/list]

[u]What I didn't like[/u]
[list]
  [*] The UI/UX
  [*] The Gameplay 
  [*] The replayability 
[/list]

[h1]Review[/h1]

 In Orwell you are an investigator, you need to investigate what might be a terrorist attack, and find the culprit(s). You can check people's background, access their emails, listen to their phone conversations or access their electronic devices. You can choose not to inform what you find to orwell or frame someone so he or she goes to jail.
 There are a couple of different endings, for both the story and the characters (including you, of course). Not all are happy.

[u]Why I liked[/u]
[list]
  [*] The Story: Is really rich, and depending on your choices, full of plot twists.
  [*] The Character Building: All the characters are really well written, how they interact between each other, and their personalities. I in part, what makes the story rich
[/list]

[u]Why didn't like[/u]
[list]
  [*] The UI/UX: You have an annoying companion, that cannot be disabled, that makes annoying comments about the data you upload. The uploading process could be faster also, I understand it tries to simulate a real computer connected to internet, but still it could be faster.
  [*] The Gameplay: Even though your choices matter, there are not a lot of choices you can make. All the data-chunks get highlighted, and the only options you have, are either uploading the information, or not. There's really no challenge, and probably by the third episode, you'll just be looking for highlighted text.
  [*] The replayability: I got all the Achievements in about 28 hours, and completed the game 4 times in that time, exploring all the endings.
[/list]

[h1]Bottom Line[h1]
 I thought I was going to find something different, something I could replay once and again. I really think the game has a lot of potential, but I can't recommend it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
ORWELL - 3/10

Quick Review:  A slightly more interactive version of a visual novel, Orwell tries to claim some of the success legendary books like 1984 and Brave New World have. Unfortunately it's cliche and boring characters, simple and tedious gameplay, long wait times and confusing target audience make this a game I can't possibly recommend.

Story
-------
You play as an investigator who is hired from outside a country where a new system called "Orwell" is put in place. In it's early stages, Orwell is being used to collect data and spy on people in order to keep the public safe. After a bomb goes off in Freedom Plaza, your job is to find who is behind the bombing by investigating someone who has a small criminal history that was at the scene and see what you can discover from there.

The story isn't particularly interesting and while there are some major plot events I don't think they hit their intended mark for me because I wasn't particularly captivated in the first place. The characters you have to investigate are all the typical "fuck the government" protesters with little to no original personality traits. Everything is unoriginal and cliche as can be.

Gameplay
--------------
Orwell is split into 5 episodes, each taking roughly around 40 minutes to an hour. You sit in front of a virtual computer screen representing the UI for Orwell, and you have to drag and drop highlighted bits of information from various pages (news articles/blogs/websites etc) in order to learn more about the people you're investigating. Some of these bits will be conflicting (highlighted in yellow, like addresses or opinions). You will have to listen in on conversations, read personal emails. You're basically just spying on people and using their profiles to learn more about them.

The gameplay is literally just drag and drop information onto the character it is relevant too. You don't even actually need to read anything because all the important information will be highlighted anyway. Conflicting information is important because it defines what happens to each character at the end of an episode but it's always easy to figure out which is right once you discover what both conflicting elements are (which the game will tell you anyway once you find both). You'll also have to listen to long, unskippable and un-fastforwadable phone calls for a tiny bit of information.

Design
---------
I think the game interface, while basic does look nice. It's entirely pale blue and means that the game doesn't feel aggressive or heavy. The soundtrack is forgettable, I turned it down pretty early to help me concentrate. The writing is actually pretty good but the characters and story is just unoriginal.

Problems
-------------
The biggest problem is that it's just boring. There barely is anything that constitutes real gameplay as all you're doing is dragging + dropping or waiting around for phone calls to end. As the story isn't very interesting (to me anyway) the further I got into the game the more of a chore it became. As I also said, almost everything is a straight appropriation of the older Orwellian style novels. I mean the game is called "Orwell". I seriously also hated having to wait around and listen to phone calls. It would've been better for the characters to have the call offscreen and you just get uploaded the transcript once you collect enough information (so phone calls would act like checkpoints; like the rest of the articles in the game do).

Achievements
-------------------
